setup.caption: 3. Line the cups up from fewest to most.

flow.do: 1. Out of sight, put 5, 8, 11 and 14 beans in four marked cups. 2. Mix up the cups. 3. Explain the rules. 4. Your child picks any two cups and partners their beans. 5. Note which cup had more. Put the beans back.
flow.say: Line these cups up from fewest to most. No counting. You may partner two cups at a time.
flow.kid: Pick two cups. Tip them out in two rows. Partner the beans. Which cup had more?
flow.parent: Keep the two rows well apart so that every bean goes back to the right cup. If beans get mixed, count them back yourself, quietly.
flow.context: This is the first step of Four Cups, a challenge where you order four cups of beans without counting. Here you compare the first two cups.

flow.do: 1. Your child compares a second pair that shares one cup with the first pair. 2. Before a third check, ask what they already know. 3. Read the usual ways and the creative ways aloud.
flow.say: Red had more than blue. Blue had more than green. Do you need to check red and green? Why?
flow.kid: Red has more than blue. Blue has more than green. What do you know about red and green?

ask.q: How can you be sure without checking?
good: Red beat blue and blue beat green, so red has even more than green.
Green's beans all have partners in blue, and blue's all have partners in red.

check.q: Red has more than blue. Blue has more than green. Which cup has the fewest beans?
check.why: Green. Blue has more than green, and red has even more than blue. Picking blue means stopping after the first clue.

flow.context: This is step 2 of Four Cups, a challenge where you order four cups of beans without counting. Here you work out one answer without checking it.

flow.do: 1. Your child makes a plan and finishes the line of four cups. 2. Make one tally mark for each partnering. 3. Do not help unless asked.
flow.say: Finish the line. I will make a mark each time you partner two cups. Let us see how few you need.
flow.kid: Finish the line from fewest to most. Use as few partnerings as you can.
flow.parent: Four cups can always be ordered with 5 partnerings. Sometimes 3 or 4 are enough. 6 means every pair was checked. Any working way is good. Fewer checks is a bonus.
flow.context: This is step 3 of Four Cups, a challenge where you order four cups of beans without counting. Here you finish the line with your own plan.

flow.do: 1. Now your child counts the beans in each cup, along the line. 2. Check that the numbers go up. 3. Ask your child to explain their plan to someone else at home.
flow.say: Now you may count. Do the numbers go up along your line? Tell me how your plan worked.
flow.kid: Now count each cup along your line. Do the numbers go up? Tell someone your plan.

ask.q: Which check did you not need to do? Why not?
good: Red and green, because I knew from blue.

flow.context: This is the last step of Four Cups, a challenge where you order four cups of beans without counting. Here you check your line by counting and explain your plan.

items.p: Which row has more dots?
items.why: Row A has more. Each dot in row B sits under a dot in row A, and row A has 2 dots with no partner.

items.p: Give each vadai one idli. ____ idlis have no partner.
items.why: 4 idlis get a vadai as a partner. 3 idlis are left over. So there are 3 more idlis than vadais.

items.p: A longer row always has more things in it.
items.why: False. A row can be long because its things are big or far apart. 5 spoons far apart make a longer row than 7 beans close together.

items.p: Which number is bigger: 9 or 6?
items.why: 9 is bigger. When you count you say 6 first and reach 9 later. On the number line 9 is further along.

items.p: One more than 7 is ____.
items.why: The next number after 7 is 8. One more thing means the next number in the count.

items.p: Put these numbers in order, smallest first.
items.why: Counting up, you say 2 first, then 4, then 5, then 8. A number you say later is bigger.

items.p: Match each pair of groups to the words that fit.
items.why: 6 and 6 leave nothing over, so they are the same. 3 spoons run out before 5 plates, so there are fewer spoons. 9 beans leave 5 over after 4 cups, so there are more beans.

items.p: There are 5 children and 5 chairs. Every child sits. What is true?
items.why: The same number. Every child has a chair and no chair is empty. Nothing is left over on either side.

items.p: Sort each number: smaller than 10, or bigger than 10?
items.why: 7, 4 and 9 come before 10 when you count, so they are smaller. 13, 18 and 11 come after 10, so they are bigger.

items.p: Draw 5 plates. Draw more than 5 spoons. Join each plate to one spoon.
items.a: 5 plates, 6 or more spoons, and one line from each plate to its own spoon.
items.why: A strong drawing has at least one spoon with no line. That spoon with no partner is what 'more spoons' means.

items.p: Draw two rows of dots with the same number. Make one row long and one row short.
items.a: Two rows with the same number of dots, one spread out and one close together.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the long row and the short row can hold the same number. Count both rows to check.

items.p: Say your answer aloud. A grown-up writes it. In the Partner Test, why did the long row of spoons have fewer?
items.a: The spoons were far apart, so the row was long. There were only 5 spoons, and 7 beans.
items.why: A strong answer says that the length of a row depends on the gaps and the size of the things, not only on how many there are.

items.p: Which is bigger: 14 or 17?
items.why: 17 is bigger. Both have one full ten. 17 has 7 more and 14 has 4 more. 7 is more than 4.

items.p: Write a number between 11 and 14: ____
items.why: 12 and 13 are both right. Each is bigger than 11 and smaller than 14.

items.p: Which number is one less than 20? ____
items.why: One less means one step back on the number line. One step back from 20 is 19.

items.p: Put these in order, biggest first.
items.why: 19 is the furthest along the number line, then 16, then 13. 8 has no full ten, so it is the smallest.

items.p: How many more dots does Arjun have than Lakshmi?
items.why: 4 more. 7 of Arjun's dots have a partner in Lakshmi's row. 4 have none. Picking 11 means counting all of Arjun's dots.

items.p: 12 is smaller than 9, because 2 is smaller than 9.
items.why: False. 12 is one full ten and 2 more. 9 does not fill a ten. So 12 is bigger than 9.

items.p: If 8 is more than 5, then 5 is less than 8.
items.why: True. The two sentences say the same fact from the two sides. If 8 has some left over, 5 is the one that ran out.

items.p: Look at each pair. Is the first number more, or less?
items.why: 15 is more than 12. 6 is less than 16. 20 is more than 19. 11 is less than 17. 10 is more than 9. Find each pair on a number line to check.

items.p: Farhan has 12 marbles. Kavya has 9. How many more has Farhan?
items.why: 3 more. From 9, hop to 12: 10, 11, 12. That is 3 hops. Picking 21 means adding the two numbers together.

items.p: Draw a staircase of dots for 3, 4, 5 and 6. Write each number beside its row.
items.a: Four rows of 3, 4, 5 and 6 dots, starting at the same edge.
items.why: A strong drawing has each row exactly one dot longer than the row above. That is what one more looks like.

items.p: Say it aloud. A grown-up writes. How do you know that 17 is bigger than 14?
items.a: Both have one ten. 17 has 7 more ones and 14 has only 4 more.
items.why: A strong answer gives a reason: the tens are the same and 7 is more than 4. Or: you say 14 first and reach 17 later.

items.p: Amma puts 2 big dosas on one plate and 5 mini dosas on another. Which plate has more?

views.says: The mini dosas. 5 is more than 2.
The big dosas. There is more to eat.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other girl has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, then says the other girl is also right about her kind of more.
items.why: Both are right. Nila compares the number of dosas. Yazhini compares how much there is to eat. First choose what you are comparing.

items.p: I am between 15 and 17. Which number am I? ____
items.why: Only 16 is bigger than 15 and smaller than 17.

items.p: I am more than 9 and less than 12. I am not 10. I am ____.
items.why: The numbers more than 9 and less than 12 are 10 and 11. It is not 10, so it is 11.

chart.title: Cover the numbers it cannot be

items.p: Red cup has more than blue. Blue has more than green. Which cup has the most?
items.why: Red. Red has more than blue, and blue has more than green. So red has more than both.

items.p: Which row has fewer dots?
items.why: Row A has fewer. Row A has 12 and row B has 13. One dot in row B has no partner.

items.p: Six 1-rupee coins or two 10-rupee coins. Which is more money?
items.why: Two 10-rupee coins make 20 rupees. Six 1-rupee coins make 6 rupees. 20 is more than 6. Picking the six coins means comparing the number of coins, not the money.

items.p: A heap of 4 big potatoes has more things than a heap of 9 small peanuts.
items.why: False. 9 is more than 4. The potato heap is bigger, but it holds fewer things.

items.p: There is a number that is bigger than every other number.
items.why: False. Name any number, and one more than it is bigger. So no number can be the biggest.

items.p: Put these five numbers in order, smallest first.
items.why: 0 stands for none, so it is the smallest. 9 has no full ten. Then 11 and 15, which have one ten. 20 is two tens.

chart.title: Find each number on the line

items.p: Match each pair of numbers to how many more the first one is.
items.why: Hop from the smaller number to the bigger one and count the hops. 7 to 10 is 3. 14 to 15 is 1. 12 to 12 is no hop. 15 to 20 is 5.

items.p: Meenakshi scored 16 runs. Arjun scored 13. Meenakshi won by ____ runs.
items.why: From 13, hop to 16: 14, 15, 16. That is 3 hops. So Meenakshi has 3 more runs.

items.p: Say it aloud. A grown-up writes. Is 10 a big number or a small number? Give one example for each.
items.a: It depends what you compare it with. 10 laddus for one child is a lot. 10 grains of rice is very little.
items.why: A strong answer says that 10 is big next to a smaller number and small next to a bigger number. No number is big by itself.

items.p: Draw 3 big circles in a long row and 6 small circles in a short row. Circle the row with more.
items.a: The row of 6 small circles is circled.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the short row holding more circles. 6 is more than 3, whatever the size of the circles.

items.p: A long row has 6 lemons. A short row has 8 beans. Which row has more?

views.says: The lemons. Their row is longer.
The beans. Two beans have no lemon.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? When could a longer row really have more?
items.a: A strong answer agrees with the girl, because partnering leaves 2 beans over. It adds that a longer row has more when the things and the gaps are the same size.
items.why: 8 is more than 6. Length depends on the size of the things and the gaps. The boy's rule works only when both rows use the same things with the same gaps.

quiz.p: One banana for each child. Are there enough bananas?
quiz.why: No. 6 bananas find 6 children, and 2 children are left with no banana. There are fewer bananas than children.

quiz.p: Every cup has one spoon. No spoon is left over. What is true?
quiz.why: The same number. Every cup has a partner and every spoon has a partner. Nothing is left over.

quiz.p: You spread 6 beans far apart. Now they are more than 8 beans in a heap.
quiz.why: False. Spreading beans out does not add any. 6 is still fewer than 8. Give each of the 6 a partner from the heap, and 2 are left over in the heap.

quiz.p: 5 big potatoes sit in a long row. 9 chana sit in a short row. Which group has fewer things?
quiz.why: The potatoes. 5 is fewer than 9. The potatoes take up more room, but room is not the same as how many.
13 is bigger. You say 8 first and reach 13 later. On the number line 13 is further along.
One less means one step back. One step back from 16 is 15.
9 is smaller. 11 is a full ten and one more. 9 does not fill a ten. Picking 11 means looking at the numerals 1 and 1, not at the ten.

quiz.p: Order these numbers from the smallest to the biggest.
quiz.why: Counting up, you say 6 first, then 10, then 14, then 19.
19 is bigger than 18 and smaller than 20. It is the only number between them on the number line.

quiz.p: How many more dots does Kavya have than Farhan?
quiz.why: 4 more. 6 of Kavya's dots have a partner in Farhan's row. 4 have none. Picking 16 means adding the two rows.

quiz.p: You have 7 runs. The other player has 9. How many more do you need to have the same?
quiz.why: 2 more. From 7, hop to 9: 8, 9. That is 2 hops. Picking 16 means adding the scores.

quiz.p: 7 is bigger than 5, and 7 is also smaller than 9.
quiz.why: True. 7 is the bigger number next to 5 and the smaller number next to 9. A number is big or small only next to another number.

quiz.p: One sheet is torn into 2 pieces. A sheet of the same size is torn into 8. What is true?
quiz.why: The sheets were the same size, so the paper is the same. Only the number of pieces differs. More pieces is not more paper.

open_questions.q: How can an elephant smell which bucket holds more seeds?
open_questions.why_open: The scientists who did the test in 2019 said that they do not yet know how the elephants do it.

open_questions.q: Do other animals have anything like our exact numbers, or only a sense of more and less?
open_questions.why_open: Animals choose well when two amounts are very different, and less well when they are close. Scientists do not agree on what this tells us about the animals' minds.

open_questions.q: How does a six-month-old baby tell 8 dots from 16, before learning any number words?
open_questions.why_open: Tests show that babies can do it. How the brain does it is still being worked out, and scientists do not agree.

open_questions.q: Is 'more' out there in the world, or does it need someone to compare?
open_questions.why_open: Mathematicians and thinkers have argued for more than two thousand years about whether such facts are found or made. No test has settled it.

maths.problem: In hand cricket, Kavya made 9 runs and Arjun made 6. Who won? By how many runs?
maths.explain: 9 is more than 6, so Kavya won. Partner the run-beans: 6 of Kavya's beans find a partner, and 3 are left over. On the number line, 6 to 9 is 3 hops: 7, 8, 9.
maths.context: In mini hand cricket you kept the score with beans and partnered them at the end. This uses the same idea with two scores.
maths.why_maths: Every match ends by comparing two numbers. The beans left over tell you who won, and by how much.

maths.problem: 8 people sit down for lunch. There are 5 banana leaves. Is there a leaf for everyone? How many more are needed?
maths.explain: Give one leaf to each person. 5 people get a leaf, and 3 people have none. So there are fewer leaves than people, and 3 more leaves are needed. 5 and 3 more makes 8.
maths.context: In Enough for Everyone you partnered tumblers with plates before a meal. This uses the same idea with people and banana leaves.
maths.why_maths: Partnering tells you at once if there is enough, and the ones left without a partner tell you how many more to fetch.

maths.problem: Three girls play kabaddi. Meenakshi scores 14 points, Lakshmi scores 9 and Farida scores 17. Put the scores in order, smallest first. Who scored the most?
maths.explain: 9 has no full ten, so it is the smallest. 14 and 17 both have one ten. 4 extra ones is fewer than 7 extra ones, so 14 comes before 17. Farida's 17 is the biggest.
maths.context: In the Bean Staircase you put number cards in order and checked them on a number line. This does the same with three scores.
maths.why_maths: Putting scores in order shows the lowest, the middle and the highest at one glance.

maths.problem: Amma puts 6 big vadais far apart on one plate. She puts 8 small vadais close together on another plate. The first plate looks fuller. Which plate has more vadais? How can you check without counting?
maths.answer: The second plate has more vadais. Check by partnering.
maths.explain: Looking at how full a plate is can fool you, because big things far apart take up more room. Put one small vadai next to each big vadai. Every big vadai gets a partner, and 2 small vadais are left over. So the second plate has 2 more.
maths.context: In the Partner Test, a long row of spoons had fewer things than a short row of beans. This uses that finding on two plates of vadais.
maths.why_maths: Knowing that room is not the same as number tells you when your eyes need a check, and partnering is the check.

maths.problem: Yazhini has 16 shells. Nila has 19 shells. Who has more? Use the ten to decide.
maths.answer: Nila has more. 19 is bigger than 16.
maths.explain: 16 is one ten and 6 more. 19 is one ten and 9 more. The tens are the same, so compare the extra ones. 9 is more than 6. So 19 is bigger than 16, by 3.
maths.context: In Two Ten-Frames you built two numbers between 11 and 20, and saw that both held one full ten. This uses the same idea with shells.
maths.why_maths: Seeing the ten inside both numbers means you only have to compare two small numbers, 6 and 9.

roots.context: We compared spoons and beans, cards and cricket scores. Now let us think about what 'bigger' and 'more' really mean.

deep_truth.truth: In the card game Bigger or Smaller, your 7 was the bigger card next to a 5. Then the same 7 was the smaller card next to a 9. The 7 did not change. So 7 is not a big number or a small number by itself. It is bigger or smaller only next to another number.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'a big number' as if big were inside the number, like the colour inside a crayon. But big and small always need two things, side by side.
deep_truth.evidence: In the game Bigger or Smaller, the same card was the bigger one in one round and the smaller one in another. On the number line, 7 is further along than 5 and not as far along as 9.

three.who_am_i: You are the big one next to a baby, and the small one next to Paatti. You did not change. Only the one beside you changed.
three.what_is_life: A lioness hears that three strangers are more than one. An elephant smells which bucket holds more seeds. Many living beings compare.
three.what_is_this_world: The Sun looks as small as the Moon. But the Sun is far bigger, and very far away. To know what is bigger, we must compare with care.

roots.thread: Think of one bean alone on a plate. Is it more? Is it fewer? You cannot say. Put a second bean on the plate, and now there is one and one more. Add many beans, and you can make rows and put them in order. So more, fewer, bigger and smaller all begin when one becomes two.

teachings.teaching: The Tao Te Ching says that long and short shape each other, and high and low rest on each other.
teachings.link: A row of beans is long only next to a shorter row. A number is big only next to a smaller number.

teachings.teaching: Thiruvalluvar, the Tamil poet, says: a help as small as a millet seed is counted as big as a palmyra palm by those who know its worth.
teachings.link: The same thing can be small by one measure and big by another. So before we compare, we choose what to compare. The two sheets of paper showed this: more pieces, the same paper.

science.text: Babies who are six months old cannot count or talk. Even so, they can tell a picture of 8 dots from a picture of 16 dots. They cannot yet tell 8 dots from 12 (Xu and Spelke, 2000). So a rough sense of more comes before number words.
Is 'more' out there in the world, or does it need someone to compare? Mathematicians and thinkers still argue about this.

other_view.who: Plato, a Greek thinker who lived about 2,400 years ago, and many mathematicians today
other_view.view: They say that 7 is more than 5 whether or not anyone compares them. It was true before there were people, and it is true everywhere. Yes, you choose whether to compare pieces or paper. But once you have chosen, the answer is fixed. You find it. You do not make it.

practice.title: Short breath, long breath
practice.say: Sit still. Take one small, short breath. Now take a long, slow breath. That second breath was long. Now take the longest breath you can. Next to this one, was the second breath still long? Nothing about that breath changed. Sit quietly for three more breaths and just notice each one.
practice.kid: Take a short breath. Now a long one. Now the longest breath you can. Was the second breath long or short?

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out what young children understand about more and fewer? This card tells the true story of a famous test, and of the scientists who questioned it.
how_we_found_out.story: About eighty years ago in Geneva, Switzerland, two scientists, Jean Piaget and Alina Szeminska, tested what young children think about more and fewer. They laid out two rows of counters, partnered one to one. The children agreed that the rows were the same. Then the scientists spread one row out. Many children under six now said the longer row had more. In a book in 1941, the two wrote that young children do not yet understand that a number stays the same when the things are moved. For years most teachers believed this. Then other scientists looked again. In 1967 Jacques Mehler and Thomas Bever tested children of two and three with two rows. Many of the youngest picked the row with more, even when it was the shorter row. In the 1970s James McGarrigle and Margaret Donaldson let a 'naughty teddy' mess up one row. Many more children now said the rows were still the same. So young children understood more than the first test showed. The way a question is asked can change the answer.
how_we_found_out.who: Jean Piaget and Alina Szeminska. Later Jacques Mehler, Thomas Bever, James McGarrigle and Margaret Donaldson
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Children under six cannot understand that a row keeps its number when it is spread out. Later tests, with a row chosen by the child and with a 'naughty teddy', showed that many young children do understand it when the question makes sense to them.

playtest: Walked through every flow as a family of two in a flat. The Partner Test needs 12 rajma, 12 chana, 5 spoons and 4 onions. Each round was laid out on paper: the leftovers are 2 beans, 5 chana, none, and 1 chana, and the katori round leaves 3. Round 4 works only if the two rows are made the same length, so the grown-up sets it out. Bigger or Smaller was dealt in the head with 2, 3 and 4 players and alone: with one set of cards there are no ties, and 10 rounds take about 5 minutes once the cards are made. Secret Number always ends, in 5 guesses or fewer if the guesser halves the strip. Mini hand cricket was tried with 1 to 3 fingers: an innings lasts at most 6 balls and 18 runs, and many innings end sooner, so play more than one match. In Four Cups, beans from two cups can get mixed, so keep the two rows well apart. Step minutes add up to each activity's minutes. Facts looked up on the web while writing: the 1994 lion study, the 2019 elephant study, the 2008 mosquitofish study, the 2000 baby study, the 1941 book by Piaget and Szeminska, the 1967 and 1974 follow-up studies, the Sun and Moon sizes, Thirukkural 104, Tao Te Ching 2 and the rules of hand cricket. The 1967 and 1974 studies were confirmed in outline only, not their exact numbers. The three videos were confirmed by title and channel only, not watched, so watch each one before showing it. The claim that a lone fish usually joins the bigger group comes from tests on mosquitofish and may not hold for every kind of fish.
